learningObjective: Distinguish unsafe collective replay after a partial optimizer commit from safe recovery at a shared checkpoint boundary.
mediumRationale: A deterministic SVG is the smallest medium that can align four rank-local states at the failure point and branch them into unsafe communication-only replay versus safe coordinated rollback. Direct state labels make the consistency invariant visible without adding runtime behavior.

mediumComparison.mermaid: Rejected: a flowchart can express the recovery branches, but automatic layout makes it difficult to align simultaneous rank-local states and show precisely which ranks applied the optimizer transition.
mediumComparison.svg: Selected: deterministic geometry keeps four ranks on one timeline, contrasts the two recovery scopes, and preserves a compact phone-width reading order.
mediumComparison.semanticHtml: Rejected: a table can list rank states but does not clearly connect the shared checkpoint, partial commit, and two divergent recovery paths.
mediumComparison.interaction: Rejected: simulating different failed ranks would add controls and state without improving the core invariant that all ranks must restart from one application-level commit boundary.
mediumComparison.paperReuse: Rejected: runtime documentation and the ULFM literature include useful architecture and API material, but no permissive license was established for candidate figures. The shipped diagram uses original geometry, wording, and a synthetic four-rank state trace.
mediumComparison.noVisual: Rejected: the prose correctly says that collective replay is insufficient, but readers must mentally track different rank-local optimizer states and distinguish communicator recovery from application-state recovery.

pages.insight: The LLM training slide mentions FSDP and mixed-precision communication, but does not discuss collectives, worker failure, rollback, or state consistency.
The mixed-precision training slide discusses numeric formats and optimizer-state memory, but not distributed failure semantics.
The training-stack slide combines FSDP or ZeRO, activation checkpointing, and other throughput techniques; its checkpointing reference is activation recomputation rather than fault recovery.
The data-pipeline system-design slide covers data availability and collection, not failed ranks or communication recovery.
The neighboring modeling slide covers task definition and baselines, with no distributed-training recovery content.
The production-serving slide covers model gating and monitoring but not training collectives or commit boundaries.

deckReview.notes: The complete 214-page local deck was text-indexed for fault tolerance, all-reduce, collectives, NCCL, process groups, rank failure, stragglers, network partitions, elastic membership, and checkpoints. It contains no dedicated fault-tolerant-collective or all-reduce slide. Pages 107, 114-115, and 166-168 were inspected as the nearest distributed-training, optimizer-state, checkpointing, and systems neighborhoods; none explains communicator failure or application-level rollback. No deck image, wording, or layout is reused.

sources.title: Elastic Agent — PyTorch documentation
sources.usage: Used as official runtime documentation to verify that fault recovery tears down all workers and restarts everyone, and that membership changes also restart the worker group.
sources.license: PyTorch documentation is BSD-3-Clause licensed through the PyTorch repository, but no documentation figure or prose is reproduced. The visual is independently authored.

sources.title: User-Level Fault Mitigation (ULFM) — Open MPI documentation
sources.usage: Used as official implementation documentation to verify failure-aware communicator operations: revoke interrupts pending communication, shrink removes failed ranks, and agree propagates failure knowledge.
sources.license: Open MPI documentation is covered by the project's BSD license, but no diagram, wording, API example, or source code is copied.

sources.title: Post-failure recovery of MPI communication capability: Design and rationale
sources.usage: Used as the primary research reference for restoring communication capability after process failure and separating MPI-level recovery mechanisms from application recovery policy.
sources.license: The SAGE journal article is publisher-controlled and no permissive figure-reuse license was identified. No paper figure, prose, or experimental result is reused.

sources.title: Distributed Checkpoint — PyTorch documentation
sources.usage: Used as official documentation to verify that distributed recovery includes model and sharded optimizer state and supports load-time resharding across cluster topologies.
sources.license: PyTorch documentation is BSD-3-Clause licensed, but no documentation figure, prose, code, or checkpoint layout is copied.

sourceReview.notes: The hardest prose-only mental model is that communicator recovery and optimizer-transition recovery have different scopes. If ranks have mixed states S_t and S_(t-1), a communication-only retry cannot infer or undo which optimizer applications committed. The original four-rank example therefore contrasts replay from mixed state with restoring model, optimizer, scheduler, scaler, RNG, and data position from one committed checkpoint before replaying the complete step.

agentReview.summary: Read the complete article, searched all 214 deck pages and inspected the nearest distributed-training neighborhoods, then checked official PyTorch, Open MPI, and distributed-checkpoint documentation plus the primary ULFM paper before selecting an original commit-boundary state diagram.

implementation.accessibility: The SVG has a linked title and detailed description narrating every rank state and both recovery paths. Rank labels, explicit S_t versus S_(t-1) notation, solid versus dashed outlines, branch headings, arrows, and written outcomes make color redundant. The 360-unit viewBox has no minimum width and uses existing 11-14 unit visual labels for readability at 390 CSS pixels. Existing theme variables preserve dark-mode contrast, and shared print rules force a light high-contrast palette and keep the figure together.
